title: Sn Atoms on Cu Nanoparticles for Suppressing Competitive H2 Evolution in CO2 Electrolysis
abstract: The electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide (CO2) to chemical feedstocks is an attractive method for the removal of CO2 from the environment. Although copper (Cu)based catalysts produce hydrocarbons with relatively high selectivity during CO2 electroreduction, such catalysts evolve a certain amount of H2 via proton reduction reactions. Because lowcoordinated Cu sites are likely active for the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER), hindering such low-coordinated Cu sites by decoration with inert metal atoms is a promising approach to increasing the selectivity of the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) over the HER. In the present study, we synthesized tin (Sn)-modified Cu nanoparticles with varied Sn ratios via a simple wet-chemical method. Physical and theoretical characterizations revealed that Sn atoms preferentially locate at the lowcoordinated sites when Sn is present at low contents (less than 1.5%). Compared with the bare Cu catalyst, the Sn-modified Cu electrocatalyst shows suppression of the HER and acceleration of the carbon monoxide (CO) evolution reaction. The first-principles calculations about the adsorption strength of reaction intermediates revealed that low-coordinated Cu sites with the modification of Sn atoms exhibited lower activity for both HER and CO2RR than that without modification. As a result, the activity of coordinatively saturated Cu atoms, where the CO2RR is more favorable than the HER, was emphasized. The modification of trace foreign metals in metal nanoparticles may provide an avenue for the synthesis of selective electrocatalysts for various target reactions.

KEYWORDS: CO2 reduction, Cu nanoparticles, low-coordinated surface sites, Sn modification, DFT calculations
■ INTRODUCTION Excessive emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2) due to the use of fossil fuels are becoming a serious obstacle to the sustainable development of society. Therefore, technologies for closing carbon (C) cycles are urgently needed.1−3 Among various methodologies for effectively reducing CO2 emissions, the electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) has attracted intensive attention because a high rate of CO2 conversion is expected even at ambient temperature and pressure.4−7 Metallic copper (Cu) has been regarded as a promising CO2RR electrocatalyst since the 1980s because only Cu-based electrocatalysts catalyze CO2 conversion to organic substrates such as methane (CH4), ethylene (C2H4), and ethanol (C2H5OH) with relatively high efficiency.
8 Consequently, numerous studies on the development of highly active and selective Cu-based CO2RR catalysts have been reported.9−16 However, the existing Cu-based catalysts still suffer from the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER),8 which competes to some extent with the CO2RR under a wide range of operating potentials. Therefore, the development of Cubased catalysts for hydrocarbon production with high selectivity over the HER is important.
Strasser et al. investigated the particle size effects of Cu nanoparticles (2−15 nm) as CO2RR catalysts in detail.13 They observed a drastic increase in the HER with decreasing Cu particle size, which was attributed to an increase in the population of low-coordinated surface sites and a decrease in the abundance of coordinatively saturated Cu atoms in terrace sites with high selectivity for hydrocarbons. On the basis of this previous report, we hypothesized that an increase in the CO2RR selectivity over the HER can be achieved through selective deactivation of the low-coordinated Cu sites. Although there are several possible approaches to deactivating the low-coordinated Cu sites, including the use of organic compounds or inorganic ligands,17−19 we herein chose to selectively modify Cu nanoparticles with HER-inactive metal atoms at their low-coordinated surface sites because we can

Tin (Sn) effectively catalyzes the CO2RR to produce formic acid (HCOOH) as the main product, with a faradaic efficiency (FE) greater than 90% and inhibition of the HER.20−22 There are several reports of Cu−Sn alloys developed as effective catalysts for the production of HCOOH or carbon monoxide (CO).23−31 For example, Cui et al. codeposited CuxSny alloys and found that the CuSn3 sample demonstrated better than 95% selectivity toward HCOOH at a low potential [−0.5 V vs reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE)].25 Haruyama et al. electrodeposited Cu−Sn alloys with different crystal structures and found that Cu87Sn13 exhibited high selectivity toward CO (60% FE at −0.99 V vs RHE), whereas Cu55Sn45 exhibited 60% FE for HCOOH.26 Most of the studies on Cu−Sn catalysts focused on bimetallic alloys with different composition ratios (i.e., Cu3Sn, CuSn, and CuSn3),
25,26,31 or control of the morphology by hybridizing Cu catalysts with Sn atoms.24,27,28 In these reports, the Sn content was greater than 10%; thus, the Cu terrace sites, which are active toward hydrocarbon production, were somewhat hindered by Sn atoms. As a result, hydrocarbon production was nearly suppressed. Because the atomic radius of Sn is substantially larger than that of Cu, the low-coordinated sites would be preferentially occupied by the Sn atoms in Cu−Sn catalysts. Therefore, Cu atoms with unsaturated coordination are expected to be selectively replaced when Sn is present at trace levels. On the basis of the aforementioned hypothesis, in the present work, we modified Cu nanoparticles with a trace amount of Sn atoms and used them as selective CO2RR catalysts working on gas-diffusion electrodes (GDEs; Scheme 1). We investigated the preferred site of the Sn atoms and the CO2RR mechanism using first-principles calculations.
■ EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Chemicals and Materials for Experiments. Copper(II) acetate monohydrate [Cu(CH3COO)2·H2O, 99%], tin(II) chloride dihydrate (SnCl2·2H2O), hydrochloric acid (HCl, 99%), methanol (CH3OH, 99.8%), potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3, 99.8%), and potassium chloride (KCl, 99.8%) were purchased from Wako Pure Chemical. Sodium borohydride (NaBH4, 99%) and Nafion solution (5 wt %) were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich. All chemicals were used without further purification. Carbon paper with a gas-diffusion layer (Sigracet 38BC) and Nafion membranes (Nafion 117) were purchased from SGL Carbon and Sigma-Aldrich, respectively. Ultrapure water obtained from a Milli-Q system (18.2 MΩ cm) was used for all catalyst preparations and electrochemical tests. Catalyst Preparation. Sn-decorated Cu nanoparticles (Cu/Sn) were fabricated via a previously reported wet-chemical reduction
method in which NaBH4 was used as the reductant. 32 Typically, Cu(CH3COO)2·H2O and SnCl2·2H2O were added to a conical flask with the desired elemental ratio and then dissolved in 250 mL of deionized water; the resultant solution was stirred for 30 min under a continuous flow of argon to remove residual O2. The total amount of metal ions was controlled to 3 mM. NaBH4 (1.14 g) dissolved into 20 mL of ultrapure water was then added to the Cu/Sn solution. The obtained black precipitate was washed with ultrapure water and C2H5OH via vacuum filtration. Finally, the prepared samples were dried at 60 °C in a vacuum oven overnight. Pure Cu or Sn samples were synthesized in a similar manner using only the Cu or Sn precursor as the starting material. The physically mixed samples were prepared by hand-mixing in a mortar the pure Cu and Sn powders that were synthesized by the above-mentioned method in the desired ratio.
Characterization. The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were recorded using a Miniflex diffractometer (Rigaku) equipped with a Cu Kα radiation source. The elemental analyses were conducted by inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectrometry (ICPOES). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM; Hitachi H9000NAR) was used for the morphological analysis. A JEOL JEM2100F microscope equipped with a high-angular annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) detector was used for TEM, high-resolution TEM (HRTEM), and selectedarea electron diffraction (SAED). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was conducted using an Axis Ultra spectrometer (Kratos Analytical) equipped with a monochromated Al Kα X-ray source. Sn K-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) for as-prepared samples was performed on the BL01B01 beamline at the SPring-8 facility (Japan). The radiation was monochromatized by a Si(311) doublecrystal monochromator. The spectra were recorded in transmission or fluorescence mode using 19 elements of germanium solid-state detectors. The Sn K-edge and Cu K-edge spectra of catalysts on the electrode after electrolysis were recorded in fluorescence mode. All XAS data were processed and analyzed using the Demeter package.33
CO2 Electrochemical Reduction Measurements. GDEs modified with the synthesized catalysts were prepared as follows. Typically, 5 mg of an as-prepared catalyst was mixed with a solution of 500 μL of CH3OH and 10 μL of Nafion, and the resultant mixture was ultrasonicated for 30 min in a tip-sonication machine to obtain a homogeneous catalyst ink. The catalyst ink was dip-coated (60 μL) onto a circular GDE to achieve a mass loading of ∼0.6 mg cm−2 and was then dried at 60 °C under vacuum prior to use.
Electrochemical measurements were performed using an electrochemical workstation (HZ-5000, Hokuto Denko) and a custom-made three-compartment electrochemical cell in conjunction with three electrodes, as reported previously.34 A Ag/AgCl (KCl-saturated) electrode and a platinum wire were used as the reference and counter electrodes, respectively. The geometric area of the working electrode was ∼1 cm2. Electrode potentials were transferred to the RHE reference scale with IR compensation. The electrolytes on the cathode and anode sides were 0.5 M KCl and 0.5 M KHCO3, respectively. The anodic and cathodic compartments were separated by a protonexchange membrane (Nafion 117, Sigma-Aldrich). The gas chamber of the three-compartment cell was bubbled with CO2 for more than 30 min before measurement. During the tests, CO2 gas was flowed at 9 sccm, as controlled by a mass flow controller. The CO2 gas with gaseous products generated throughout the experiments was collected in a gas bag and subsequently injected into a gas chromatograph using a gastight syringe. The CO2RR products were sampled after 30 min or 1 h of electrolysis.
Analysis of the CO2RR Products. The gas products were analyzed using gas chromatography−mass spectrometry (GC−MS; GCMS-QP 2010 Plus, Shimadzu, Japan) with helium as the carrier gas; the instrument was calibrated using H2, CO, CH4, and C2H4 samples diluted with CO2 to various concentrations. The liquid product was quantified by NMR spectroscopy (Varian 500 MHz, Agilent) using a presaturation method reported elsewhere.35 A 0.5 mL sample of the electrolyte after electrolysis was mixed with 0.1 mL of

The DFT calculations performed to determine the stabilization energies (Estab) of Sn atoms on the Cu surface and adsorption energies (ΔEads) for reaction intermediates were calculated using the PHASE/0 code.36 The generalized gradient approximation of the Perdew−Burke− Ernzerhof model and projector-augmented-wave (PAW) method were used. In the calculations, a slab model with three layers of Cu atoms was used (for details, see the Supporting Information). Throughout the calculations, only the bottom layer of Cu was fixed; other atoms, including adsorbates, were free to move in all directions. The atomic relaxations were conducted until the maximum force on any atom was less than 0.01 eV Å−1. The cutoff energy for the planewave function was set to 25 Ry. A k-point sampling of a 3 × 3 × 1 Monkhorst−Pack mesh was used. The vacuum space was greater than 15 Å. The Estab for Sn atoms was calculated as follows using a Cu(553) surface:

■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Physical and Morphological Characterization of Cu/ Sn Catalysts. We fabricated Cu/Sn catalysts with various Sn contents (0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 5, and 10 atom %), as well as bare Cu and Sn nanoparticles, by tuning the ratio of the precursors (Scheme 1a). The bulk composition of the catalysts was quantified by ICP-OES (Table 1); the results show that their
atomic composition was similar to that of the added precursors. The obtained catalysts are denoted as Cu/Sn-x, where x indicates the atomic ratio (%) of Sn precursors. The crystalline structure of the as-prepared catalysts was analyzed by XRD (Figure 1). We observed peaks at 30.0°, 36.7°, 42.7°, 43.3°, 50.6°, and 61.6°, which are attributed to the Cu2O(110), Cu2O(111), Cu2O(200), Cu(111), Cu(200), and Cu2O(220) planes, respectively.
42 In addition, some samples showed small peaks assignable to CuO, which might be derived from the oxidation by air. These results indicate that the dominant crystal phases of these samples were a mixture of Cu and Cu2O. The XRD results show no Sn-related peaks with increasing Sn content, even at a Sn content of 10%, indicating that crystalline Sn agglomerates, such as Sn metal nanoparticles or oxides, did not form on the Cu/Cu2O
nanoparticles during the synthesis.26 Furthermore, the intensity ratio and peak area (Table S1), which are related to different crystal facets, are almost same with the increasing Sn contents, which means that Sn modification on Cu nanoparticles has no impact on the preferred crystal orientation.15
We next investigated the morphologies of the Sn-modified Cu samples by TEM imaging (Figure 2). The particle size of the Cu and Cu/Sn catalysts was ∼20 nm for both. Detailed (S)TEM investigations and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) mappings were conducted for further structural characterization and observation of the distribution of elements, respectively. Representative (S)TEM images and the corresponding EDX mapping images for samples Cu/Sn0.5, -1.5, and -10 are shown in Figures 2 and S1 and S2. The HRTEM images (Figure S2b) indicate good crystallinity of the Cu/Sn-1.5 catalyst, with a Cu2O(111) d spacing of 0.240 nm, consistent with the XRD results.11,43 The SAED patterns can also confirm a distinct structure of the Cu2O/Cu mixed phase (inset image of Figure S2e). The atomic-scale-resolution STEM−EDX mapping images (Figure 2g,h) show a homogeneous distribution of Sn atoms and few Sn aggregates (>1 nm) on the Cu/Sn-0.5 and -1.5 samples. With increasing Sn content, the EDX mapping images of the Cu/Sn-10 sample show phase separation between the Cu and Sn parts, indicating that Sn agglomerates formed on the Cu agglomerates (Figures 2i and S3). The direct observation of atomically dispersed Sn atoms in Cu/Sn catalysts using STEM is in progress in our laboratory. We next investigated the electronic states of the Cu and Sn species in Cu/Sn catalysts using various X-ray techniques. Parts a and b of Figure 3 show XPS narrow-region scans for Cu 2p and Sn 3d, respectively. In Figure 3a, the peaks at 932.4 and 952.4 eV, which are assignable to Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2, are clearly observed, suggesting that the Cu(0) and/or Cu(I) valence state(s) was (were) dominant, although a small portion of Cu(II) was observed in the deconvoluted curves (Figure S4).44 These results basically correspond to the XRD results. The peaks at 486.0 and 494.5 eV in the spectrum of the Cu/Sn-0.5 sample are assigned to Sn 3d5/2 and Sn 3d3/2, respectively (Figure 3b). The Sn 3d peaks of the Sn-decorated Cu nanoparticles shift to higher binding energies by ∼0.65 eV when the Sn content is increased from 0.5% to 10%. The peak top positions for Sn d3/2 and d5/2 finally reach 486.6 and 495.1 eV, respectively, which are positions similar to those of Sn

nanoparticles synthesized without Cu. These XPS results reveal that the electronic states of Sn atoms decorated on Cu/Cu2O nanoparticles are slightly reductive compared with the electronic states of Sn atoms in SnO2.
45 X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectra corresponding to the Sn K-edge (Figure S5a) were recorded to obtain further insight into the electronic state of Sn atoms in Cu/Sn catalysts. The onset of the normalized XANES curves for Cu/Sn catalysts (20207.0 eV) corresponded with that for SnO2, indicating that
the Sn(IV) oxidative state is dominant for all Sn species in Sndecorated Cu/Cu2O nanoparticles.
46 In contrast, the valence state of Sn atoms in the physically mixed Cu/Sn catalysts is zero, as confirmed by the XANES spectra (Figure S5b). Figure S5c shows Sn K-edge extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) spectra for Cu/Sn catalysts, and the fitting results of EXAFS are summarized in Table S2. The coordination number of the first coordination sphere containing O atoms (the peak at 1.7 Å) for Cu/Sn catalysts is smaller than that for SnO. In

addition, the peak at 3.5−4.0 Å assignable to the second coordination sphere observed in SnO2 is rarely observed. These results are basically consistent with the reported EXAFS for Sn nanoclusters containing O and OH as anions.47,48 Taken together, the TEM and EXAFS results show that oxidized Sn nanoclusters were formed on Cu/Sn catalysts with a high Sn concentration. We speculate that a relatively higher Debye− Waller factor for a Cu/Sn catalyst with higher Sn loading is due to the low crystallinity of Sn nanoclusters on Cu nanoparticles. To confirm the Sn species in physically mixed Cu/Sn catalysts, we analyzed the Fourier-transformed EXAFS of those samples (Figure S5d). The peak assignable to Sn−Sn (2.9 nm) is clearly observed for physically mixed Cu/Sn catalysts. This result indicates that Sn species in physically mixed Cu/Sn catalysts dominantly exist as Sn(0), although the top surface might be partially oxidized by air. On the basis of the aforementioned XRD, STEM−EDX, and
XPS results, we explain the electronic states and morphology of the Sn atoms on Cu/Cu2O nanoparticles as follows. At low Sn contents (less than 1.5%), most of the Sn atoms are atomically dispersed, with a valence state of IV. As for the as-prepared samples, atomically dispersed oxidized Sn atoms would be grafted onto CuxO layers with O or OH ligands.
49,50 As the Sn ratio increases (greater than 1.5%), oxidized Sn nanoclusters might be formed on the Cu/Cu2O nanoparticles, and the Sn 3d peaks shift toward the positive energy region. Finally, when the Sn ratio reaches 10%, most of the Sn is aggregated as oxidized Sn nanoclusters. CO2 Electrolysis Performance of Cu/Sn Catalysts. The CO2 reduction behavior was investigated using a homemade three-compartment cell with the GDEs carrying the Cu/Sn catalysts (Scheme 1b and Figure S6). Cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves of the Cu/Sn electrode are compared with those of bare Cu catalysts (without Sn modification) in a 0.5 M KCl electrolyte solution under continuous CO2 supply conditions (Figure S7). Although the onset potential of the cathodic currents was approximately −0.38 V versus RHE, little difference was observed in the onset potentials among the Sn-decorated Cu samples with molar ratios between 1.5% and 5% and the bare Cu sample. The Cu/Sn-0.5 and -10 samples exhibited slightly more positive (−0.25 V vs RHE) and slightly more negative (−0.47 V vs RHE) onset potentials, respectively, than the other Cu/Sn-x samples. We next analyzed the products of the CO2RR carried out under galvanostatic conditions (j = 200 mA cm−2). The FEs of the reduction products are shown in Figure 4. The FEs of H2 as the product of proton reduction reactions decreased to less than 15% upon the addition of just 1.5% Sn atoms, whereas the FE of bare Cu nanoparticles was ∼25%. Focusing on gaseous CO2RR products, we found that the amount of CO, which has been reported elsewhere to be the main product obtained with most Cu/Sn alloy catalysts,17 clearly increased when Cu was modified with a trace amount of Sn (<5%). Notably, the sum of the FEs for hydrocarbons (CH4 and C2H4) showed almost no decay for the Cu/Sn-0.5 and -1.5 samples when compared with the sum of the FEs for bare Cu nanoparticles. In particular, the FE of CH4 formation increased for the Cu/Sn0.5 and -1.5 samples. When the Sn content was greater than 5%, the main product was HCOOH. The FE for HCOOH formation for the Cu/Sn-10 catalyst reached 40%. We also discuss the roughness factor of the electrodes and turnover frequency (TOF) in Figures S8 and S9 and Table S3.
The CO2RR potential dependence for the bare Cu and Cu/ Sn catalysts is shown in Figure 5. Parts a, c, and e of Figure 5 indicate that Sn modification suppressed H2 evolution over the full range of examined potentials. With respect to the partial current density of various products (Figure 5b,d,f), the H2 partial current density decreased to approximately −12.4 mA cm−2 from −41.7 mA cm−2 under a potential of −1.25 V versus RHE upon modification of the Cu nanoparticles with 1.5% Sn. The current density of CH4 reached −27.5 mA cm−2 at a potential of −1.25 V versus RHE for Cu/Sn-1.5. Notably, it has been reported that CuxO can be reduced at −0.3 V versus RHE. Therefore, the Cu surfaces are reduced to Cu(0) during CO2RR electrolysis.
51,52 In addition to Cu, the oxidative Sn atoms are also known to be easily reduced to Sn(0) at about −0.3 V versus RHE.53,54 Therefore, both oxidized Cu and Sn atoms in the as-prepared samples are instantaneously reduced to metallic states with zero valences during CO2RR electrolysis. Next, we conducted stability tests of Cu/Sn-0.5 and -1.5 catalysts at a constant current of 200 mA cm−2. The FEs for H2 and CO generation were almost constant, and thus the doping effect of a trace amount of Sn to Cu particles was maintained for 6 h (Figure S10). These results suggest that our Sndecorated Cu catalysts were stable enough to discuss the effect of Sn doping within this time scale. Figure S11 shows the XAS analyses for Cu/Sn catalysts after electrolysis. Although no obvious change in the spectra was observed for Sn atoms by electrolysis, we could not exclude the effect of air oxidation after electrolysis. Thus, analysis of the electronic states of Cu and Sn by operand XAFS measurement is an essential future work. We also tested the CO2RR performance using physically mixed Cu/Sn samples as reference samples with the same molar ratios (Sn % = 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 5, and 10; Figure S12). As expected, the physically mixed Cu/Sn samples exhibited almost no change in the product composition when the Sn content was low. Thus, modification with Sn atoms played a critical role in suppressing H2 formation and enhancing CO generation.
DFT Analyses of the Position of Sn atoms and the Catalytic Mechanism. As shown in Figures 4 and 5, at low Sn contents (less than 1.5%), the FE of the HER was suppressed to approximately half of that with bare Cu nanoparticles, resulting in an increase of the FE of the CO2RR to CO. Here, we consider the mechanism underlying
https://doi.org/10.1021/acsanm.1c00514 ACS Appl. Nano Mater. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
E
these unique catalytic activities. To verify the details of the catalytic mechanism, the structure and location of Sn atoms should first be identified. The STEM results show that the Sn atoms were atomically dispersed in the as-prepared catalysts with trace Sn contents. However, as mentioned above, CuxO and the oxidized Sn atoms were reduced to the metallic state under CO2RR experiments. Thus, we next attempted to investigate where the Sn atoms are located in the Cu/Sn catalysts during electrolysis using stabilization energy (Estab) analyses via DFT calculations.23,55 In the present work, the Cu(553) facet was adopted as the model structure because the structure possesses both coordinatively saturated and unsaturated sites. We calculated Estab for eight different positions of Sn atoms in Cu(553), as shown in Figure 6. Figure S13 shows the structures after relaxation for four Sn-substituted Cu(533).
In Table 2, we list Estab values for the Sn atoms in Snsubstituted Cu(553) using the value for the Sn atom
substituted into a low-coordinated site (site a) as a standard (for details of the calculations, see the Experimental Section). The Estab value of a Sn atom substituted into the lowcoordinated site (site a in Figure 6) of the Cu was 0.25−0.37 eV smaller (more stable) than that of a Sn atom substituted into the first layer of saturated Cu sites on the surface (sites b− d in Figure 6). Thus, Sn atoms exist more stably on unsaturated sites of Cu nanoparticles than on saturated sites. In addition, the Sn atoms in the second layer of Cu(553) (sites e−h) are much more unstable than those in the first layer. These DFT calculation results reveal that Sn atoms tend to preferentially locate at low-coordinated surface sites of the Cu nanoparticles. Next, DFT analyses were performed for CO2 reduction to CO, which is the intermediate of CH4 and C2H4, and for the HER. For calculation of the adsorption energies, Cu(100) and Cu(211) were adopted as the model structures of clean flat surface and low-coordinated Cu sites, respectively (Figure S14). We calculated the adsorption energies of the intermediates on the Cu atoms of bare Cu(100) and Cu(211) and on the Cu and Sn atoms of Sn-doped Cu(211), which are denoted as Cu@Cu/Sn and Sn@Cu/Sn, respectively. First, we investigated the HER activities for the four adsorption sites by obtaining the corresponding Gibbs free energy diagram (Figure 7a). The bare Cu(100) and Cu(211) facets show H* formation energies of 0.50 and 0.004 eV, respectively. These results indicate that the HER at the

atom on Cu(211) (Sn@Cu/Sn) shows a H* formation energy of 0.71 eV. This result indicates that H* adsorption onto Sn atoms is endergonic and that atomically dispersed Sn sites cannot function as active centers for the HER because of weak interaction with H*, consistent with previous reports.23 In addition, a low-coordinated Cu site in Cu/Sn (Cu@Cu/Sn) exhibited a H* formation energy of −0.1 eV. This result indicates that the rate-determining step for the HER at Cu@ Cu/Sn became the desorption of H2 molecules and that modification of Sn decreased the HER activity on the neighboring Cu sites. We next investigated the CO2RR for CO generation at the low-coordinated sites. The formation energies of the CO2RR intermediates for CO generation at −0.8 V versus CHE are shown in Figure 7b. The reaction free energies are summarized in Table S4. The CO desorption barriers (ΔGCO) for Cu(211), Cu@Cu/Sn, and Sn@Cu/Sn (less than ∼0.2 eV) are certainly lower than those for the reported materials suffering from CO poisoning.56,57 Besides, the generation of CO molecules from the adsorbed COOH* is thermodynamically favorable by more than 1 eV. In this case, CO poisoning effects are known not to be serious.57 Thus, the rate-determining step would not be CO desorption but the formation of COOH*. The formation energy of COOH* (ΔGCOOH) is almost 0 eV on the lowcoordinated sites of bare Cu(211); this formation energy is the lowest value among the four investigated adsorption sites. The ΔGCOOH values on Cu@Cu/Sn and Sn@Cu/Sn are 0.08 and 0.64 eV, respectively. Therefore, not only the CO generation activity on Sn sites but also that on neighboring Cu sites is suppressed by the modification of low-coordinated Cu sites with Sn atoms, which is similar to our findings related to the

To understand the selectivity between the HER and CO2RR, we plotted the limiting potential of CO2RR for CO generation (UL,CO2RR, which corresponds to the limiting potential of COOH* formation in the present study) and the HER (UL,HER) in Figure 7c. The authors of the previous reports 40,58 used UL,CO2RR − UL,HER as a descriptor of the selectivity of CO2RR over HER; thus, a more positive value for UL,CO2RR − UL,HER indicates greater selectivity for the CO2RR. The values of UL,CO2RR − UL,HER for the Cu(100) and Cu(211) surfaces are −0.47 and −0.79 V, respectively, indicating that the CO2RR selectivity on the coordinatively saturated Cu sites on the Cu(100) facet is greater than that on the low-coordinated sites on the Cu(211) facet. This consideration is consistent with the previous experimental results related to Cu nano-

■ SUMMARY OF THE DEPENDENCE OF THE HER AND CO2RR ACTIVITY ON SN AMOUNTS
On the basis of the aforementioned DFT calculations, the mechanism responsible for the change in the FEs of the HER and CO2RR upon Sn modification is summarized as follows (a schematic is shown in Scheme 2). Both the HER and CO2RR are more active at Cu atoms in unsaturated (i.e., lowercoordination-number) sites, such as kinks, steps, and edge sites, than those in saturated (i.e., higher-coordinationnumber) sites, such as terrace sites, on pure Cu nanoparticles, as shown in Figure 7. In the case of Cu/Sn catalysts with a lower Sn content (less than 2.5%), some of the Cu atoms in low-coordinated sites are preferentially replaced by Sn atoms. Considering that Sn atoms served as the active centers for CO or HCOOH production in the previous papers,59 the Sn sites would exhibit higher selectivity for the CO2RR against HER. However, the DFT results indicated that the HER and CO2RR activities at the low-coordinated sites modified with Sn atoms are lower than those at the site without modification. As a result, the activity of saturated Cu sites, where CO2RR is more favorable than HER, is relatively emphasized with such lower contents (less than 2%). Importantly, the saturated Cu sites still remain and function as active centers for the further reduction reaction, leading to CO; thus, the FEs of CH4 and C2H4 for Cu catalysts with trace amounts of Sn were approximately comparable to those for Cu nanoparticles. Considering the DFT results and CO partial current density, an important question arose: although the DFT results suggested that both the HER and CO2RR activity decreased by the substitution of Cu atoms by Sn atoms, why did the CO partial current density increase (Figure 5)? Not only CO2RR but also HER produced OH−, and then OH− reacted with the CO2 substrate to electrochemically inert (bi)carbonates. Therefore, the HER at low-coordinated sites would decrease the CO2 concentration at the catalytic surface, resulting in pure Cu showing a lower CO2RR current density than Cu/Sn catalysts. Indeed, it has been reported that CO2 absorption as carbonates by the local pH effect cannot be neglected under these high current conditions in neutral solutions using GDEs60 (70% of the consumed CO2 was absorbed as carbonates in the previous paper). When we further increased the Sn content (greater than 1.5%), Sn atoms were modified onto not only the unsaturated sites of Cu nanoparticles but also the saturated terrace sites or even formed oxidized Sn nanoclusters, as suggested in the TEM−EDX results in Figures 2i and S3. The saturated Cu sites decorated with foreign metal atoms would not be active toward C2H4 and CH4 production.
13 Thus, increasing the Sn content to greater than 1.5% would decrease the FEs of hydrocarbon species such as CH4 and C2H4. Oxidized Sn nanoclusters are known to generate HCOOH; thus, the Cu/Sn catalysts with higher Sn loadings can more effectively produce HCOOH than pure Cu or Cu/Sn catalysts with a lower Sn content. As for the reported Sn-doped Cu catalysts, the Sn concentration is relatively high (>10%) compared with that of our catalysts.25,31 Therefore, even the coordinatively saturated
Cu sites were likely substituted by Sn atoms, resulting in the production of only CO or HCOOH.
■ CONCLUSION In this work, we prepared Cu catalysts with various molar ratios of Sn and confirmed the formation of different Sn moieties when the Sn content was varied. The Cu/Sn catalysts with a low Sn content (less than 1.5%) exhibited better CO2RR selectivity, which led to higher FEs of CO production and almost the same FEs of hydrocarbon production. In particular, the Cu/Sn-1.5 sample showed a CH4 partial current density of −27.5 mA cm−2 at −1.25 V versus RHE. DFT calculations confirmed that the Sn atoms preferentially decorated the low-coordinated sites of the Cu particles. The H2 evolution biased unsaturated sites decorated with Sn atoms suppress the FEs of H2 production, which is beneficial for the CO2RR-active saturated Cu sites. We expect these results to provide guidance in the search for other effective CO2RR catalysts by modifying Cu crystals with various elements at extremely low contents. In addition, this methodology could be applied generally to other metal nanoparticles with unique electrocatalytic properties.
